In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the following problems: (i) the problem of finding the number of spanning subgraphs in a graph; (ii) the problem of determining the number of spanning trees in a graph; and (iii) the problem of enumerating the number of spanning cycles in a graph.
the study of tournaments and their bypaths, which are paths that contain a given arc and are disjoint from a specified arc.

the following questions. What is the maximum number of cycles of length k in a tournament on n vertices, for k and n large? What is the minimum number of cycles of lengths k and k+1 in a tournament on 2n vertices, for k large and even?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
if T is a 3-connected regular tournament with n vertices then every arc of it has a bypath in T of length n - 2, unless n ⩽ 8.

a 3-connected regular tournament with no 3-cycles contains an arc with a bypath of any length greater than or equal to 3 if and only if it is not isomorphic to the two tournaments mentioned in the abstract.
a regular tournament of order n ⩾ 4 is Hamiltonian if and only if n ⩽ 7, n ⩾11 or n = 10, and that a regular tournament is Hamiltonian if n ⩾12.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found a way to construct a large number of 3-regular tournaments with a given cycle structure, which is the same as the cycle structure in the tournament of Alspach, Hsu and Liu (1989).
we have found a new way to solve the problem of finding all the tournaments with the given properties.
we are able to prove that if every arc of a $k$-connected tournament $T$ is contained in a $k$ cycle, then every arc has a $k$ bypath, for all $k \geq 3$.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the existence of a large number of cycles with a common length in a tournament implies the existence of a lot of cycles with other lengths.
the structure of a 3-arc-connected tournament is not very different from the structure of a regular tournament.
the study of bypaths in tournaments has a rich history and that the problem is still open for many interesting cases.
